A Gigantic Stellar Eruption Spreads Planetary Material Into Space

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1629 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that highly-evolved stars spread the material for upcoming planets and stars into space with their stellar winds.
  • In a recent development, the material is first emitted in pulses of gas, and eventually that gas cools into dust and the star's radiation pressure pushes it away with its stellar wind.
  • According to recent reports, researchers at Chalmers University in Sweden have been observing Mira, an AGB star about 300 light years away.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that highly-evolved stars spread the material for upcoming planets and stars into space with their stellar winds. These stars are called aysmptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, and they're cool, luminous stars that are running out of hydrogen and leaving the main sequence behind. As they age, they can shed as much as 30 Earth masses of material per year into the interstellar medium (ISM).

In a recent development, the material is first emitted in pulses of gas, and eventually that gas cools into dust and the star's radiation pressure pushes it away with its stellar wind. Carbon and silica are important parts of what's emitted, and silica is the main building block for rocky planets, while carbon feeds into organic particles. So these stellar winds from AGB stars clearly play an important role in the formation of planets, other stars, and even potential life.

According to recent reports, researchers at Chalmers University in Sweden have been observing Mira, an AGB star about 300 light years away. It's the prototype and namesake of what are called Mira variables, pulsating AGB stars that are oxygen-rich. Their results are challenging the long-held understanding that stellar winds driven by radiation pressure are what spread heavy elements into the interstellar medium (ISM).

Industry observers note that the research is "A giant magnetic eruption from the asymptotic-giant-branch star Mira A," and it's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics. The lead author is Wouter Vlemmings, Professor in the department of Physics and Astronomy at Chalmers University of Technology in Gothenburg, Sweden.

Industry observers note that "Mass loss during the advanced evolutionary stages of low- and intermediate-mass stars is traditionally attributed to dust-driven winds, whereas the influence of magnetic fields remains poorly constrained," the authors write. "This mass-loss process is crucial for the chemical enrichment of the Universe.".

Since this type of mass-loss is so fundamental, it's attracted a lot of attention and is the subject of a huge amount of research. In this work, the researchers used the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) observations to study how Mira's magnetic fields might shape its mass loss. ALMA can't directly observe magnetic fields; instead it observes them indirectly through their polarizing effect on radio emissions.

In a recent development, âFor decades, astronomers have believed that the winds from stars like this must be powered by starlight. Light from the star shines on grains of dust in the starâs outer atmosphere, and that gives them a push. But this star is showing us something different: that strong magnetic fields can also shape and power stellar winds. That changes a fundamental part of the origin story of the atoms we ourselves are made of," lead author Vlemmings explained in a press release.

This schematic shows the structure of an AGB star, from its degenerate core to its circumstellar envelope. It shows it during its thermal pulse stage, when pulses drive gas outward, where it cools and forms dust in the envelope. Radiation pressure generates the stellar wind that drives the dust away into the ISM. Image Credit: Lu et al. Front. Astron. Space Sci., 23 July 2025. Sec. Astrostatistics.

Recent findings suggest that astrophysicists have detected strong magnetic fields in the circumstellar envelopes of AGB stars like Mira, and researchers have suggested that they may play a role in driving their mass loss. But the researchers explain that there's been no empirical evidence of the role magnetic fields play in the process, and that wind-driven mass loss models don't include magnetic fields.

Recent findings suggest that recent observations, however, are challenging the overall understanding of the wind-driven mass loss scenario. Some AGB stars show mass-loss but also show insufficient dust to explain it. These stars are oxygen-rich AGB stars like Mira. Since Mira is the nearest of its type of dusty, pulsation-driven O-rich AGB stars, it makes sense to study it.

Both ALMA and the Very Large Array recently observed Mira A, the AGB star, and its companion Mira B, a white dwarf, in August 2025. But observations go back ten years, and both sets of data combine to reveal dramatic changes on Mira A's surface.

"During the past decade, high-angular-resolution observations of Mira A at visible, millimetre, and submillimetre wavelengths have revealed several unexpected phenomena related to the stellar atmosphere and mass-loss process," the authors write.

This ten-year study of Mira's surface is the longest study of any star other than the Sun.

Recent findings suggest that this time-lapse shows ten years of changes on the surface of Mira A. Credit: W. Vlemmings et al. 2026. Astronomy and Astrophysics.

âWe were astonished to see how the starâs surface is constantly changing. The brightest areas were different every time we looked, and the brightest patches are amazingly bright. We realised that star is flaring, releasing vast amounts of energy each time," remarked study co-author Miora Andriantsaralaza, a postdoctoral researcher in the department of Physics and Astronomy at Chalmers University of Technology.

Recent findings suggest that some of the hotspots in the video have brightness temperatures of 8,000 Kelvin. That's far higher than the average 2,000 K brightness temperature.

But the main finding is what researchers call SiO (silicon monoxide) masers. They're often found in the circumstellar envelopes of AGB stars, just inside the dust formation zone. But Mira A's masers are at a much greater distance, where the gas is too thin for a strong SiO maser to form. So the researchers say the masers trace a shock moving outward, and that it has much higher density than expected. In short, a flare that expanded into a huge loop of expelled material.

Sources indicate that âIn 2023, we saw one of these flares appear on the starâs surface, but it didnât stop there. Over the next two years, this eruption on the surface created a vast, expanding loop of gas around the star, which we captured in an image in 2025. The loop was much bigger than the star, extending as far out as the distance of Saturn from the Sun. We hadnât seen anything like that before," said co-author Behzad Bojnordi Arbab, a doctoral student at Chalmers University.

In a recent development, masers aren't always polarised, but these ones are linearly and circularly polarized. Linearly polarised means its polarisation is organized, and the polarising is shaping it. Circular means it rotates in a corkscrew pattern. Taken together, the astronomers used those features to map Mira's magnetic field geometry. That in turn let them understand how the magnetism is shaping its wind and its mass loss.

The loop and its polarisation is the key in this work.

It has been revealed that âIn the loop, thereâs a strong magnetic field, which must also influence the starâs wind. That showed us a connection between the flare and the loop, and reminded us also of phenomena we can see on our Sun," said Vlemmings.

It has been revealed that this figure from the research shows a three-dimensional representation of the adopted magnetic-loop ejection model anchored to the surface of Mira. The structure is colour coded according to line-of-sight velocity. Image Credit: W. Vlemmings et al. 2026. Astronomy and Astrophysics.

In a recent development, for now, the source of these magnetic fields isn't entirely clear. "The origin of the magnetic fields responsible for the observed ejections remains uncertain, although several mechanisms have been proposed," the authors write. A turbulent dynamo deep in Mira's convective envelope could be responsible, or differential rotation between the star's core and envelope could be behind them. Making progress understanding how the magnetic fields drive mass loss will depend on understanding how they're generated.

The flares and magnetic fields are evidence of a newly introduced element in mass-loss. On our Sun, flares are generated by magnetic fields, and they're associated with coronal mass ejections, where material is sent speeding away from the Sun. But our Sun is young, and isn't an aged AGB star experiencing the same level of mass loss. Still, these findings draw a parallel between the two.

Industry observers note that âNow we see that magnetic storms on Miraâs surface are continually creating bright flares. Even more surprisingly, each of these is strong enough to lift parts of the starâs outer layers and launch them into interstellar space,â stated Andriantsaralaza.

This research indicates that our understanding of AGB mass-loss has to take into account magnetic fields, not just radiation-driven stellar winds.

It has been revealed that "The discovery of coronal-mass-ejection-style eruptions from an AGB star redefines our understanding of late-stage stellar evolution," the authors write. They can help explain some of the features of AGB mass-loss, like clumpiness, asymmetry, and time variability. They can also help explain some of the morphologies of planetary nebulae, the beautiful shells of ionized gas ejected by aged stars.

Sources indicate that "Consequently, magnetic activity must be integrated into models as a dynamically dominant force in initiating mass loss and shaping circumstellar environments," the authors conclude in their study. And since AGB mass loss spreads the stuff of planets into the ISM, that could explain, at least partly, why we're here.

It has been revealed that âOur study has consequences for our understanding of the whole of the galaxyâs ecosystem. Perhaps, Earth wouldnât be here if it wasnât for magnetic storms on a red giant star, billions of years ago before the Sun was born," mentioned Vlemmings.

#191784. Voyager 1's light-day milestone: See the photos behind the discoveries

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1484 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Livescience ↗ Open Full Page

Voyager 1's light-day milestone: See the photos behind the discoveries

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1484 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Livescience

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a new space exploration milestone: The probe, which launched in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth.
  • The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.
  • The growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Early Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a new space exploration milestone: The probe, which launched in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth.

The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.

The growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe. But with Voyager 1 still collecting data with two of its science instruments, which are expected to stay powered up into the 2030s, NASA scientists say one thing is certain: The spacecraft isn't done surprising us.

Sources indicate that "What Voyager has taught me is to expect the unexpected," Linda Spilker, who joined the Voyager team in 1977 and is the mission's current project scientist, told Live Science in an interview. "So many times the ideas and theories we had, Voyager was able to prove them wrong.".

Here, we look back at some of Voyager 1's most groundbreaking discoveries, told through its incredible photos.

NASA's Voyager 1 probe debuts atop a Titan/Centaur-6 launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

It has been revealed that NASA's Voyager 2 probe introduced before Voyager 1, on Aug. 20, 1977. Voyager 1 took off a few weeks later, on Sept. 5. (The two spacecraft took slightly different routes through the solar system, allowing Voyager 1 to reach interstellar space first after a gravity boost from Jupiter and Saturn.).

Spilker, who joined NASA right out of college, attended the historic Voyager 2 launch and recalls "that feeling of watching the rocket lift up off the launchpad, feeling the roar of those rocket engines and knowing this was a mission going to visit places I'd always been curious about.".

A few weeks after launching, Voyager 1 took this photo of a crescent Earth and moon from 7.25 million miles (11.66 million km) from Earth.

On its way to the outer solar system, Voyager 1 snapped this image of a crescent Earth and its moon, captured in the same frame for the first time ever.

In a recent development, voyager 1 photographed Jupiter from January to April 1979, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As the spacecraft zoomed closer to the giant planet, it snapped an image every 96 seconds, creating this incredible time-lapse animation of the planet's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of one Earth month.

Sources indicate that the close-up view showed that Jupiter is a far more dynamic world than previously thought. But Voyager also made key discoveries about the planet's many moons.

Sources indicate that while passing by the Jovian moon Io, Voyager 1 witnessed an explosion: the first volcanic eruption ever seen beyond Earth. This proved that there were other geologically active worlds in our solar system, opening up entirely new avenues of inquiry and exploration.

A blue eruption on Jupiter's moon Io, the first volcanic eruption seen on another world.

"Going in, we thought that the moons would look a lot like our own moon: ancient dead worlds," Spilker noted. "And yet we found out they were very different worlds — like Io with active volcanoes. It was just an incredible change in our thinking.".

Industry observers note that by viewing these eruptions, scientists saw parts of Io's surface being changed in real time. "As we got closer [to Io], scientists kept saying the surface is getting younger and younger, because they didn't see any major craters, no medium sized craters, no little craters — until finally parts of its surface are just minutes old," Spilker mentioned.

A mosaic view of Callisto taken from Voyager 1 photos at a distance of about 250,000 miles (400,000 km).

Recent findings suggest that some of Voyager's close-up observations also confirmed old theories. For example, Voyager 1's flyby of the moon Callisto in March 1979 revealed vast fields of well-preserved impact craters, proving that Callisto was geologically dead.

Jupiter and its thin ring of dust backlit by the sun in a Voyager 1 image.

Recent findings suggest that A final surprise at Jupiter came when Voyager 1 swooped around the planet's nightside, seeing the gas giant backlit by the sun. This view revealed a thin ring system around the planet, made partly of the dust particles Io spewed into space.

It has been revealed that voyager 1 reached Saturn in November 1980 and made its closest approach to the planet on Nov. 12 of that year. Four days later, the spacecraft took this image of the planet's nightside, showing a broad shadow cast onto the surrounding rings.

It has been revealed that "That is one of my favorite pictures: an outbound image, taken by Voyager looking at [Saturn] in a way you could never see from the Earth," Spilker noted, noting that we can only ever see Saturn's sunlit side from our planet. "The rings just look so beautiful shining there, and you can actually see the shadow of Saturn on the rings themselves. It's a really, really special picture.".

In addition to discovering a previously unknown ring, Voyager 1 spotted five new moons around Saturn and took close-up photos of several other known satellites.

Voyager 1's closeup view of Titan revealed a dense, hazy atmosphere.

Recent findings suggest that the mission required Voyager to swing by the moon Titan in order to bend the probe's trajectory, sending it away from the solar system's planetary plane and toward a rendezvous with interstellar space. Before that, Voyager 1 revealed Titan's atmosphere to be so hazy that it completely obscured the moon's surface. This demonstrated that Titan's clogged atmosphere was far denser than those of Earth and Mars.

Recent findings suggest that by 1990, Voyager 1 was so far from the planetary plane that our solar system's planets looked like little more than specks of light. But before turning off its camera for good, Voyager 1 looked back at our cosmic neighborhood and took some of the most iconic space photos of all time.

In a series of 64 images taken from roughly 40 times Earth's distance from the sun, Voyager snapped its solar system "family portrait," a mosaic of images capturing six planets together for the first time. The portrait included views of Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Frames from Voyager 1's family portrait showing Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

The image of Earth from this collection is famously known as the "Pale Blue Dot.".

Sources indicate that "We took the pictures of the planets in color, and that one is especially one of my favorites," Spilker said. "There's Earth captured in a sunbeam. A tiny world less than a pixel in size representing all the life that we know in our solar system — just a very special image reminding us just how special and precious our planet is.".

Earth appears as a pale blue dot in this iconic Voyager 1 image.

It has been revealed that voyager 1 turned off its camera immediately after taking these images, concluding its role as the greatest tourist in the history of our solar system. In 2012, Voyager 1 passed beyond the heliopause — the boundary where the sun's radiation gives way to the interstellar medium — becoming the first interstellar spacecraft in history.

According to recent reports, voyager 2 crossed the same boundary in 2018 and is expected to reach its own light-day in 2035. In the meantime, several science instruments remain active on both probes, allowing them to measure the strange and mysterious environment between stars.

Even way out there, the probes are still detecting whispers of the sun's power.

"We are still seeing effects from the sun that come out, hit the heliopause, and send shocks and pressure fronts out into the interstellar medium," Spilker said. "I wonder where we will finally reach the point where the sun doesn't influence what we're seeing, and we're in the pristine interstellar medium — and I hope that happens while Voyager 1 is still operating.".

One Tiny Protein Change Could Help Explain Severe Childhood Epilepsy

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have uncovered a previously unknown molecular mechanism that helps position a protein linked to severe childhood epilepsy within nerve cells.
  • A single change in a protein associated with severe childhood epilepsy can dramatically alter where it resides inside nerve cells, according to fresh research from the University of Liverpool.
  • According to recent reports, the study focuses on CDKL5, a protein essential for normal brain development and function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have uncovered a previously unknown molecular mechanism that helps position a protein linked to severe childhood epilepsy within nerve cells.

A single change in a protein associated with severe childhood epilepsy can dramatically alter where it resides inside nerve cells, according to fresh research from the University of Liverpool. The discovery suggests that some neurological disorders may arise not only from impaired protein activity but also from proteins failing to reach the locations where they are needed.

According to recent reports, the study focuses on CDKL5, a protein essential for normal brain development and function. Mutations in the gene that produces this protein cause CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD), a rare genetic condition characterized by severe seizures beginning in infancy and significant developmental difficulties. The disorder affects approximately 1 in 40,000 to 60,000 live births worldwide.

Despite years of research into CDKL5, scientists have struggled to understand how the protein is organized within nerve cells and why certain mutations have such devastating neurological consequences.

A research team led by Ben Goult, Professor of Mechanistic Cell Biology at the University of Liverpool, identified a previously unknown molecular docking mechanism that anchors CDKL5 to the structural framework of synapses, the specialized junctions through which nerve cells communicate.

In a recent development, disrupting this anchoring mechanism altered the organization of nerve cells. The researchers also discovered that even a remarkably small modification to the protein could interfere with its positioning.

Dr. Yasumi Otani, first author of the study and former PhD student in the Institute of Systems, Molecular and Integrative Biology, said: “What was particularly striking was that changing just a single amino acid at the very end of CDKL5 was enough to dramatically alter its localization in nerve cells. This shows just how critical the final residues of the protein are for keeping CDKL5 in the right place at synapses.”.

Industry observers note that the researchers also uncovered an unexpected connection between CDKL5 and the mechanical forces generated within cells. CDKL5 binds directly to talin, a protein capable of changing its shape in response to physical forces.

Sources indicate that in experiments using cultured cells, interfering with this molecular interaction or reducing the forces produced by the cells changed the distribution of CDKL5. The findings suggest that cellular mechanics may help regulate where CDKL5 carries out its biological functions.

Recent findings suggest that many genetic mutations associated with CDD produce shortened versions of the CDKL5 protein that lack the newly identified docking sequence. These mutations may therefore disrupt neurological function partly by preventing CDKL5 from reaching its intended location, rather than solely by impairing its enzymatic activity.

Industry observers note that professor Ben Goult said: “Much of the research into CDKL5 deficiency disorder has focused on the activity of the enzyme itself. Our work highlights another potentially crucial factor: where that activity takes place. By identifying the molecular interactions that position CDKL5, we can begin to understand how the protein is organized within synapses and why disrupting this organization might interfere with communication between nerve cells.”.

It has been revealed that the research, conducted in collaboration with scientists at the University of Helsinki in Finland, establishes a molecular framework for investigating how defective protein positioning contributes to CDD. It also opens a potential avenue for therapeutic research, although whether restoring CDKL5 localization could improve neurological function remains unknown.

Recent findings suggest that andreas Borg, founder of CURE5, a parent-led foundation dedicated to finding a cure for CDKL5 deficiency disorder, remarked: “Seeing how profoundly CDKL5 loss affects so many systems in the body also gives us hope that latest opportunities for therapeutic intervention remain to be discovered. The new understanding of the protein’s location and function identified in this work opens up one such possibility. As parents, even the smallest improvements in our children’s lives mean the world.”.

Reference: “Cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) binds talin and is anchored at the postsynaptic density by direct PDZ interactions” by Yasumi Otani, Emily Goodall, Vignesh Srinivasan, Neil J. Ball, Samuel F. H. Barnett, Youlim Hwang, Dominic P. Byrne, Tobias Zech, Juha Saarikangas and Benjamin T. Goult, 20 November 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aed3338.

If you find cleaning your house to be a drag, robot vacuums do some of the dirty work for you. These intuitive little machines keep your floors tidy by vacuuming up dust, food crumbs, pet hair, and more—all without requiring you to lift a finger. They’re the ultimate “set it and forget it” cleaning solution because with robot vacuums, there’s no longer a need for you to lug around a heavy canister or upright vacuum.

Robot vacuums have come a long way in recent years. Today’s models are smarter, faster, and more capable than ever before. Many have the ability to map your home’s layout, create custom cleaning routines, and empty their own dustbins.

According to recent reports, they’re also packed with sophisticated sensors to avoid stairs and furniture, dodge socks and dog toys, and skirt past other obstacles. Some models also include mopping functionality for complete floor care. And app and voice control allow you to start, stop, and schedule your vacuum to run from anywhere.

According to recent reports, below, we’ve gathered some valuable tips on what to look for in a robot vacuum and how to use these devices. Plus, find out how we tested the top robot vacuums and which one is best for you.

For models that we tested in-house, we set up three 8-by-8-foot pens, each with a different floor surface, to simulate various cleaning scenarios for each robot vacuum. One pen featured low- to medium-pile carpet. The second had bare, polished concrete, and the third had laminate flooring. We set a stool, floor mat, and ottoman on the concrete to act as common obstacles found in the home.

Recent findings suggest that in each pen, we also scattered flour, dried rice, and crushed up cereal to represent different types of dirt and detritus. This stress test pushed the vacuums beyond typical maintenance cleaning, so we could assess how they handle more material compared to an average encounter.

According to recent reports, to better understand how these robot vacuums functioned in everyday environments, we sent several models home with staff members and testers for real-world experience. This allowed us to confidently evaluate how each device handled household challenges like pet hair, kids’ messes, and varying floor types.

Our testers used the vacuums for a month or more, assessing them based on key criteria like features, cleaning effectiveness, navigation capability, ease of use, and overall value. Although these selections were not subjected to standardized lab testing, our recommendations are grounded in hands-on experience and long-term use.

In a recent development, we are continuously refining this list to reflect the latest advancements in robot technology. Our ongoing updates show our commitment to providing trustworthy, up-to-date guidance and selections that are relevant. As newly introduced components are introduced and we test more models, we always carefully evaluate and incorporate these insights to help you choose the right tools for maintaining a clean and comfortable home.

Like its predecessor, the QV 35A is a dual system that both vacuums and mops, but it increases suction power up to 8,000 Pascals—1,000 more than the Qrevo S—for stronger cleaning performance. In a recent development, beyond cleaning performance, the QV 35A uses LiDAR navigation to scan and mop your home, creating detailed layouts within the companion app. It stores up to four floor prepares, making it a practical option for multi-story households. The app also supports a range of customization features like scheduled cleanings, custom routes. and real-time machine monitoring.

To support all of this, the highly capable docking station is designed for lower maintenance. It holds 2.7 liters of dry debris and 4 liters of water, allowing for several weeks of use before needing attention. Taken all together, these features suggest the QV 35A should perform similarly to the Qrevo S, which handled laminate, concrete, and medium-pile carpet effectively during our previous testing.

It has been revealed that she does mention that while this is a smart device and the app is advanced, it’s a little overwhelming to deal with. Industry observers note that many robot vacuums overlap in features and capability, and there are newer and better models releasing all the time. In a recent development, navigation is key to how well a robot vacuum performs its job. Suction matters little if the vacuum fails to cover every part of your floor. Just about all models utilize three fundamental types of sensors to help them navigate.

Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR).

In a recent development, this navigation method involves a laser that locates features by sending out pulses of light and measuring how long they take to return. LiDAR is especially useful for creating accurate maps and is the most powerful and most common navigation tool for robot vacuums.

With this navigation style, the vacuum travels in one direction and then changes course when it hits an object. A lot of models are programmed to optimize their paths and make them more efficient. By running into a wall in a couple of places, the robot vac can verify the location of the wall and move parallel to it, turning 180 degrees each time they hit an end wall.

Visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (vSLAM).

In a recent development, this triangulates position by tracking multiple points in a room in successive camera frames. Over time, the vacuum learns and becomes more efficient by relying on points that remain constant and do not change.

According to recent reports, suction power, which indicates how strongly a vacuum pulls in air and debris, is typically listed by the manufacturer in pascals (Pa). The bulk of modern vacuums offer anywhere from 4,000 to 10,000 Pa, but with each new model that comes out, we’re seeing those numbers continue to rise, with some upwards of 20,000 Pa. Just be aware that higher suction impacts a robot vacuum’s battery life and noise levels.

It has been revealed that A brand’s claims about suction power may not provide the full picture, either. Manufacturers don’t tell us exactly where or how they’re measuring—they may take measurements at the impeller or without passing the filter, or using the vacuum only in a controlled environment. It’s similar to how automakers disclose horsepower ratings on cars as an engine spec. The transmission, differential, and other components all leech some of that horsepower, so what’s actually available at the rear wheels differs from the number listed in the specs.

A large dustbin and water tank capacity are ideal for significant homes or households with pets, since they reduce how often you need to empty or refill. For smaller spaces or light daily cleaning, a more compact unit with a capacity of 2 liters should still get the job done. For models that also mop, a clean and dirty water tank of 4 liters or more combined is sufficient for cleaning larger areas efficiently without constant refilling. The models on our list hold between 2.5 and 5.3 liters of debris.

Beyond navigation and suction power, today’s robot vacuums come packed with bells and whistles that elevate them beyond the basic models of the past. Room mapping, self-emptying dustbins, voice assistant compatibility, cleaning schedules, and no-go zones have all become more or less the standard.

Industry observers note that the most tech-forward robot vacuums offer AI-powered obstacle recognition that identifies and steers clear of pet waste, shoes, or cables. There are also variations that have dual functionality, combining both vacuum and mopping qualities. As you might expect, the more advanced sensors and assets a robot vacuum offers, the higher its price tag.

According to recent reports, throughout our testing process, we discovered that while the mopping features are certainly useful, they don’t fully deliver the type of power or pressure needed to get rid of tough stains or set-in messes. The docking stations are also made for water only, and it’s not recommended to use any kind of detergents or DIY solutions in the robot. Some brands make their own cleaners that you can purchase separately, but make sure its compatible with your specific model. If you’re dealing with really stubborn grime, we recommend keeping a standard mop on hand.

Industry observers note that look out for shoelaces, string, carpet fringe, and thin or lightweight clothing—all of which gets easily caught in brushes and rollers. Some units have sensors that stop them when the brushes meet resistance, and some move in reverse, spitting out whatever they pulled in. This technology isn’t foolproof, so it’s best to just keep the area clear.

According to recent reports, additionally, be aware of pet bowls, plant stands, or other things that could tip over until you know how the robot vacuum interacts with them. Models that leverage bump-and-go navigation may knock things a little harder, so it’s a good idea to set up boundaries to avoid those obstacles.

In a recent development, lastly, if you have kids, many robot vacuums are capable of picking up small toys (or parts of toys) that are strewn about. A lot of units have the ability to create exclusion zones, so make use of them, or employ your own strategy to avoid all these little hazards that could jam up the vacuum.

Most homes have places where a robot won’t reach, like in between narrowly spaced furniture legs or tight corners. Also, some types of dirt and debris overwhelm robot vacuum filters, since their capacities are pretty small. Fine dust, fireplace ash, and powders, even in moderate quantities, could clog a filter and affect performance.

When set on a consistent schedule, robot vacuums help your house look clean on a day-to-day basis. Still, it’s best to run your upright or cordless stick vacuum for deeper cleans and bigger messes.

Sources indicate that place the robot vacuum and docking station in an open space that’s close to a power outlet. The power connection is essential for charging the vacuum and running automatic dustbin emptying features. When the space in front of the docking station is open and obstacle-free, the vacuum is able to tackle dirt more frequently. Try to avoid putting the unit near high-pile carpeting, near stairs, or cluttered spaces.

It has been revealed that for homes with high foot traffic, pets, or children, running your vacuum on a daily basis is ideal. Three to four times a week is best for homes with moderate foot traffic, and if you live in an apartment, or your home has multiple spare rooms that don’t get used very often, running your robot vacuum weekly (or simply as needed) will suffice.

Most units have physical controls on the vacuum to start, stop, and send the vacuum back to the docking station. However, smart features like app control, scheduling, mapping, and voice assistants require internet connection. We recommend connecting the vacuum to your home network to get the most out of these features.

A Brief-ish History of METI. Part IV: Millennial METI Experiments

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that welcome back to our ongoing series on the Brief-ish History of Messaging Extraterrestrial Intelligence (METI).
  • Today, we'll look at experiments conducted since the end of the Space Age and the turn of the century.
  • This era also saw revitalized efforts to search for signs of past (and maybe present) life on Mars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that welcome back to our ongoing series on the Brief-ish History of Messaging Extraterrestrial Intelligence (METI). In our previous installments, we examined the inspiration and earliest experiments in this field. We then looked at how it co-evolved with the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI), leading to the first true attempt to send a message of greeting to the stars (the Arecibo Message). We followed up with a look at two of the brightest minds in the business (Frank Drake and Carl Sagan), the brains behind the first interstellar messages (the Pioneer Plaques and the Voyager Golden Records).

Today, we'll look at experiments conducted since the end of the Space Age and the turn of the century. And just like SETI, the number of experiments has grown considerably, thanks to renewed interest in space exploration following new efforts to explore Mars and the Solar System. This included the first orbital observatory, the venerable Hubble Space Telescope, and deep space probes like the Galileo, Cassini-Huygens, Magellan, and Venus Express missions.

This era also saw revitalized efforts to search for signs of past (and maybe present) life on Mars. These included orbiters like the Mars Odyssey and Mars Express missions, and rovers and landers like Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner, as well as Spirit and Opportunity. These experiments also reflected the changing nature of space exploration, which included missions from emerging space agencies, non-profits, and private entities.

All of these experiments built on the legacy of the Arecibo Message, adding additional information and personal touches where the creators desired.

According to recent reports, an explanatory diagram of a message transmitted in 1983 by Masaki Morimoto and Hisashi Hirabayashi to Altair. Credit: ShizuShizu/Wikimedia.

Recent findings suggest that in 1983, astronomers Masaaki Morimoto and Hisashi Hirabayashi used the Stanford Dish radio telescope at Stanford University to transmit the Message to Altair (or the Call to the Cosmos 83'). The message was produced in collaboration with the Japanese publication Weekly Shonen Jump and transmitted on August 15th, 1983, to commemorate the publication's 15th anniversary. The destination was Altair, an A-type blue-white giant star located 16.7 light-years from Earth, which represents the Shinto deity Hikoboshi in the Tanabata legend.

In a recent development, like the Arecibo Message, the content was a symbolic, graphic message meant to convey information about humanity, life on Earth, and peace. Unlike the Arecibo message, the Message to Altair consisted of several pages rather than a single, long pictograph, each dealing with a different subject. The first page included mathematical information, such as the numbers 1 to 12, prime numbers, powers of 3, formulas for indicating addition and multiplication, and chemical elements essential to life.

According to recent reports, for this, Morimoto and Hirabayashi chose hydrogen, helium, carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen, the building blocks of stars and planetary systems. Several other molecules were included, including hydroxide, water, nitrous oxide, formaldehyde, hydrogen cyanide, and their respective wavelengths. All of these chemicals play a central role in prebiotic chemistry and the formation of organic molecules that give rise to life.

According to recent reports, page two included information on the Solar System, including (from top to bottom) the Sun, the planets in order of distance, some of the larger moons, and their equatorial radii and mean distances from the Sun. Pages three and four included the chemical formulae for DNA compounds, as well as showing DNA structure and replication. This was followed by a series of drawings that demonstrated different types of life forms on Earth, and they were arranged to convey the process of biological evolution.

They begin with pictures of early primitive life, followed by jellyfish, fish, amphibians, lizards, early mammals, apes, and then humans. Like the Pioneer Plaques, this image demonstrates a man and a woman with two children between them. This was followed by a close-up illustration of the woman's face waving hello. The last page demonstrated the transmission parameters: the total number of bits, the transmission wavelength, and the radius of the radio telescope that beamed the message.

It also contained the Japanese and English spelling for the word "toast," followed by the chemical formula for ethanol alcohol - in short, the message concludes with the raising of a toast with an alcoholic drink.

The thirteen pictures that make up the Message to Altair, listed in order (left to right, top to bottom). Credit: Shinya Nurasawa.

As Altair is approximately 17 light-years distant, the message would have arrived around 2000, and the window for a reply would open by 2017. In 2023, Hyogo University astronomer Shin-ya Narusawa (who knew Morimoto before his death) asked the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) to help search for a possible reply. JAXA obliged and used the radio antenna at the Usuda Space Observatory to observe Altair for an hour at 10 p.m. on August 22nd, 2023.

The date was significant because it also fell on Tanabata in the old Japanese calendar and is the only day of the year when the deities Orihime and Hikoboshi (represented by Vega and Altair, respectively) are allowed to meet. The observations detected no signals, but Narusawa said he intends to continue observing and collaborating with other research institutions.

Recent findings suggest that between 1999 and 2003, three METI experiments were conducted using the Evpatoria Planetary Radar (EPR), a Soviet-era facility located in the Crimea for deep-space communications and radio astronomy. All four projects were organized with help from famed Soviet-Russian radio engineer, astronomer, and SETI researcher Alexander Zaitsev. As we addressed in part I of the series, he coined the term METI in his 2006 paper, Messaging to Extra-Terrestrial Intelligence.

The first project to use the EPR RT-70 radio telescope was the Cosmic Call, which included two broadcasts, one sent in 1999 and the other in 2003. The venture was a crowdsourced effort by Texas-based startup Team Encounter, Canadian astrophysicist Yvan Dutil, Russian scientists (including Zaitsev), and Eastern European radio engineers.

In a recent development, the message included contributions by Dutil and his fellow physicist StÃ©phane Dumas. Their primer was inspired by Hans Freudenthal's 1960 book Lincos: Design of a Language for Cosmic Intercourse, which describes a language designed to be understandable to an extraterrestrial intelligence (ETI). Using Lincos, Dutil and Dumas' message (DDM) was carefully structured to include pictograms showing mathematics, physics (the hydrogen spectrum), and related concepts.

Industry observers note that the second part consisted of a series of pictograms created by Richard Braastad of Team Encounter, the Braastad Message (DM). It used mathematical symbols to describe a solar sail (another project Team Encounter was working on), including its dimensions, payload, trajectory, and projected launch time. This was followed by the original Arecibo Message (AM), the company's Team Encounter 2001 Staff Message (ESM), and a message composed with input from the public - the Public Part (PP).

It has been revealed that the second page of the primer prepared by Dutil and Dumas, denoting mathematical concepts (part of the Cosmic Call). Credit: Dumas, S.

Industry observers note that the broadcast was broken into four sessions, lasting a total of 40 hours, with each session targeting a different Sun-like (G-type) star system. These included 16 Cygni A on May 24th, 1999, a G-type star in a triple-star system located 69 light-years from Earth. On June 30th, 1999, the target was 15 Sagittae, another G-type star about 58 light-years from Earth in the Sagittarius Constellation. Lastly, and again on June 30th, 1999, the team transmitted to HD 178428, a G-type star located 69 light-years away, also in the Sagittarius Constellation.

Recent findings suggest that each session of Cosmic Call 1 transmitted the scientific parts (DDM, BM, AM, and ESM) three times at 100 bits per second, followed by the Public Part (PP), sent once at 2000 bits/s. The full message was structured as:.

DDM â BM â AM â ESM â DDM â BM â AM â ESM â DDM â BM â AM â ESM â PP.

It has been revealed that the second Cosmic Call, in 2003, followed a similar structure. For this message, Dutil and Dumas presented an updated version of their Lincos pictographs (DDM2), the Arecibo Message, the Bilingual Image Glossary, and the same Public Part. The structure was as follows:.

They included GJ 49, a G-type star located 32 light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia, on July 6th, 2003. This was followed by Gliese 208, an M-type (red dwarf) star 37 light-years away in the constellation Orion; 55 Cancri, an M-type star 41 light-years away in Cancer; HD 10307, a binary star system with a G-type primary and an M-type companion 42.6 light-years away in Andromeda; and 47 Ursae Majoris, a G-type star located 45.3 light-years away in Ursa Major.

Recent findings suggest that the Cosmic Calls were the most ambitious public SETI/METI effort mounted to date. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Metal foam explored for armor could also make everyday cars safer, with simulations suggesting it could absorb dangerous impacts without adding extra weight.
  • Industry observers note that in a head-on collision, a car’s front rails must bend and collapse in a controlled way to help protect the people inside.
  • Industry observers note that A upcoming study suggests that replacing conventional front rails with a lightweight metal foam could significantly improve crash protection, especially at higher speeds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Metal foam explored for armor could also make everyday cars safer, with simulations suggesting it could absorb dangerous impacts without adding extra weight.

Industry observers note that in a head-on collision, a car’s front rails must bend and collapse in a controlled way to help protect the people inside. These structures receive impact energy from the bumper and are designed to keep the vehicle from slowing too abruptly. Sudden deceleration can cause severe injuries, including head injuries.

Industry observers note that A upcoming study suggests that replacing conventional front rails with a lightweight metal foam could significantly improve crash protection, especially at higher speeds. Using detailed computer simulations, researchers found that the material absorbed impact energy more effectively than two common designs used in modern vehicles.

Industry observers note that the material, known as composite metal foam (CMF), contains hollow metal spheres embedded in a metallic matrix. The spheres can be made from metals or alloys such as steel, creating a structure that is lightweight and capable of withstanding substantial compression and impact. Researchers have also explored its potential use in aircraft wings, vehicle armor, and body armor.

“CMF is lighter than conventional metals without sacrificing strength, and our work here tells us that its unique structure allows it to better absorb energy during high-velocity impacts,” says Afsaneh Rabiei, corresponding author of the study and a professor of mechanical and aerospace engineering at North Carolina State University. “This is crucial because it slows the rate at which a vehicle decelerates during a crash – and slowing deceleration improves driver and passenger safety.”.

To evaluate its potential, the researchers compared front rails made from an aluminum tube with a steel CMF core against two conventional designs. One consisted of a long, hollow rectangular steel structure. The other used two hollow aluminum octagons stacked on top of each other, known as a double-octagonal design.

The team built computational models using extensive experimental data on CMF alongside publicly available information about conventional rail materials and designs. They then simulated high-speed frontal collisions to examine how effectively each structure managed the impact.

At 55 mph, CMF rails of the same weight and length reduced maximum deceleration by approximately 38% compared with double-octagonal rails. Overall crash severity fell by about 45%, while the Head Injury Criterion (HIC), a measure of the likelihood of serious head injury, also decreased by roughly 45%.

Industry observers note that the improvements were even greater when compared with rectangular rails. At the same impact speed, CMF reduced maximum deceleration by approximately 84%, overall crash severity by 94%, and HIC by 83%.

It has been revealed that the simulations also indicated that vehicles equipped with CMF rails could withstand substantially higher impact speeds before reaching critical safety limits. Compared with double-octagonal rails, vehicles could travel about 34% faster before reaching the critical crash-severity limit and approximately 40% faster before reaching the head-injury limit. Against rectangular rails, those increases were about 32% and 48%, respectively.

“CMF outperformed the conventional rails across the board,” Rabiei indicates. “And the higher the speed, the better the CMF performed compared to the conventional front rails. Comparing front rail performance during a 55 mph crash offers a good overview of the difference between designs.”.

Importantly, the simulated safety improvements did not require heavier or longer front rails. The CMF structures matched the conventional designs in both dimensions and weight, suggesting that manufacturers might eventually improve crash protection without compromising fuel economy.

“This also means that you could reduce the length of the front rails, still improve safety, and also make the vehicles more fuel efficient,” Rabiei claims.

Sources indicate that the material could also have applications in electric vehicles. Previous research has demonstrated CMF’s resistance to heat and fire, making it a potential candidate for structures designed to protect high-voltage battery packs from damage during collisions.

The findings are based on computational modeling, and physical testing would be needed to determine how CMF rails perform in actual vehicles. The researchers hope to work with manufacturers to explore these possibilities.

“We are open to working with the automobile industry to conduct testing of rails that make use of CMF in their existing front rail designs – or to develop fresh rail designs that make use of CMF to improve safety and fuel efficiency,” states Rabiei.

Sources indicate that “We are also interested in working with automakers, suppliers and battery manufacturers to evaluate CMF-based structures for electric vehicles, including battery protection systems. CMF’s combination of lightweight impact-energy absorption and resistance to heat and fire creates opportunities to address multiple vehicle safety challenges with a single material system.”.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “Enhancing Safety and Crashworthiness of Vehicles Using Composite Metal Foam” by Aman Kaushik and Afsaneh Rabiei, 2 September 2026, Journal of Composites Science. DOI: 10.3390/jcs10090474.

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

According to recent reports, more U.S. women are taking menopause hormone therapy, fresh prescription data suggest.

In a recent development, monthly dispensing of hormone therapy for women aged 40 to 74 more than doubled since 2023, growing from 2 million to 4.9 million, researchers report November 19 in JAMA. The analysis of U.S. pharmacy dispensing data revealed that this increase began in 2024. The rise continued in 2025, before and after the Food and Drug Administration’s November removal of the black box warning from packaging, and into 2026.

Although the data in the fresh study are aggregate, the researchers used population data to estimate the dispensing rate for this age group, which jumped from 28 prescriptions per 1,000 women to 67 prescriptions per 1,000 over the period studied.

It has been revealed that the newly introduced study wasn’t designed to determine what’s behind the increase. It’s possible that the evidence regarding hormone therapy’s safety and effectiveness for the treatment of menopause symptoms, such as hot flashes, is reaching more women. Medical groups such as the Menopause Society have recommended menopause hormone therapy for women with symptoms who are younger than 60 or within 10 years of the start of menopause, absent certain risk factors including prior breast cancer and stroke.

In a recent development, “Greater attention to women’s health, updated medical guidance supporting individualized menopause hormone therapy and social media may all be contributing to increased interest,” indicates Dana Sarnak, who studies sexual and reproductive health at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. Anecdotally, her clinician colleagues report more patients seeking menopause care, she says.

Many women and physicians turned away from hormone therapy in the early 2000s after a large study called the Women’s Health Initiative raised safety concerns, which were later considered overblown. Research since then has provided a more nuanced understanding of the benefits and risks of menopause hormone therapy at different ages.

There are safer formulations, including patches and gels, of estrogen today then at the time of the Women’s Health Initiative, for which participants took a pill. The fresh study found that product use increased for transdermal and vaginal estrogen and for progesterone products — women who have their uterus need to take progesterone along with estrogen. The use of oral formulations remained stable. There has been a shortage of estrogen patches in the United States this year, which the U.S. Food and Drug Administration attributes to increasing demand.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Powerful laser pulses could transform the crystal structure of a metal without first heating its atoms.
  • In a study published in Physical Review Materials, researchers led by Dr.
  • Sources indicate that when an intense laser pulse strikes a metal, its electrons absorb energy far more rapidly than its atoms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Powerful laser pulses could transform the crystal structure of a metal without first heating its atoms. Fresh research suggests that rapidly exciting electrons can make entirely different atomic arrangements energetically favorable, revealing an alternative way to control the structure and properties of metals.

In a study published in Physical Review Materials, researchers led by Dr. Sam Azadi modeled 17 elemental metals exposed to extreme electronic temperatures. Nearly all were predicted to undergo one or more solid-to-solid phase transitions driven by electronic excitation, potentially within a fraction of a picosecond (one trillionth of a second).

Sources indicate that when an intense laser pulse strikes a metal, its electrons absorb energy far more rapidly than its atoms. This creates a temporary state in which the electrons reach extremely high temperatures while the atomic lattice remains relatively cold.

It has been revealed that under these conditions, a phenomenon known as electronic entropy can determine which crystal structure is most stable. Electronic entropy describes how electrons are distributed among available energy states. As electronic temperatures rise, changes in this distribution can alter the relative stability of competing crystal structures without requiring conventional heating of the atomic lattice.

Industry observers note that “Our results suggest that electronic entropy should be regarded as a thermodynamic control parameter in its own right. Just as external pressure can transform one crystal structure into another, strong electronic excitation can reshape the free-energy landscape and create entirely new phases of matter,” noted Dr. Sam Azadi, Research Associate in Theoretical Physics.

Using advanced computer simulations, the researchers calculated how increasing electronic temperatures affect the free energy of metals, a thermodynamic quantity that helps determine which structures are most stable. They identified transitions involving several common crystal arrangements, including hexagonal close-packed (hcp), face-centered cubic (fcc), and body-centered cubic (bcc) structures.

Sources indicate that in general, hotter electrons favored crystal structures with lower densities. The researchers attributed this tendency to electronic thermal pressure, which arises as electrons gain energy.

In a recent development, some metals, however, displayed more complex behavior. Differences in the distribution of electronic states near the Fermi level, an crucial energy reference in metals, can influence which atomic arrangements become favorable under intense excitation.

In a recent development, the predicted transitions occur on femtosecond to picosecond timescales, making them potential targets for experiments using ultrafast X-ray or electron diffraction. These techniques could allow scientists to track changes in atomic arrangements immediately after laser excitation and test the theoretical predictions.

If confirmed experimentally, the findings could enable researchers to use carefully controlled laser pulses to temporarily switch metals between crystal structures, accessing material properties that are difficult to achieve under ordinary conditions. Such capabilities could have applications in ultrafast electronics, high-energy physics, and advanced manufacturing.

According to recent reports, reference: “Electronic-entropy-driven solid-solid phase transitions in elemental metals” by S. Azadi, S. M. Vinko, A. Principi, T. D. Kühne and M. S. Bahramy, 9 April 2026, Physical Review Materials. DOI: 10.1103/nzv9-dskm.
