General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Petunias reveal an unexpected link between flower color and scent

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1299 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists studying petunias discovered that the same biological machinery responsible for flower color also shapes their scent.
  • Petunias use the same raw ingredient, an amino acid called phenylalanine, to make pigments and many of their scent compounds.
  • Researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem found that a protein called EOBV works with two proteins involved in pigmentation to regulate the flower’s scent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists studying petunias discovered that the same biological machinery responsible for flower color also shapes their scent.

Petunias use the same raw ingredient, an amino acid called phenylalanine, to make pigments and many of their scent compounds.

Researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem found that a protein called EOBV works with two proteins involved in pigmentation to regulate the flower’s scent.

When the researchers removed this protein, the flowers released more compounds associated with the smell of cloves and vanilla.

However, they released less methyl benzoate, normally the most abundant scent compound in these petunias.

Industry observers note that oded Skaliter and Alexander Vainstein ran all of it in petunias. The chemistry moved. Nobody has checked whether a nose, human or moth, can tell the difference.

Wild petunias have different ways of attracting pollinators. One species releases its fragrance at night to attract moths, another attracts bees with purple flowers, and a third uses red flowers to attract hummingbirds.

Petunia pigment is run by a committee of three, known to biologists as the MBW complex.

According to recent reports, two of these proteins, AN1 and AN11, remain the same. The third can be any one of several proteins belonging to a family called MYB, and its identity determines which genes the group controls.

Skaliter and his colleagues examined when AN1 and AN11 were most active.

Activity peaked as the flowers opened and remained high for another two days, around the same time that scent production reached its peak.

Sources indicate that then they knocked each gene down, one at a time, with a plant virus. Air from around the petals went into the analyzer.

Both treatments increased the release of eugenol and vanillin. The amount of methyl benzoate roughly doubled.

Rather than helping the flowers produce more fragrance, the pigment proteins appeared to hold scent production back.

The researchers suspected that the missing piece of the puzzle was the third protein in the group.

Six MYB proteins were already in the frame here, all of them previously linked to petunia fragrance.

It has been revealed that each went up against AN1 and AN11 in yeast cells that change color when two proteins bind. EOBV was the only hit.

The team repeated the experiment in living plant tissue. This time, they used a system that produces betalain, the red pigment found in beets, when proteins interact.

It has been revealed that leaves of a tobacco relative turned red when they received both AN1 and EOBV. Leaves that received AN1 alone produced a weaker color signal.

The strongest red color appeared when all three proteins were present. Removing any one of them greatly reduced pigment production in the test.

According to recent reports, AN11 and EOBV would not bind each other. AN1 had to stand between them.

The researchers also found very little EOBV gene activity outside the petals. Within the petals, activity was about 1.8 times higher in the upper surface layer, through which fragrance escapes.

Previous work from the same laboratory found that a gene responsible for giving petals their identity also activates scent production.

According to recent reports, the next step was to remove EOBV completely. A virus carried CRISPR gene-editing tools into petunia tissue, and the team recovered three groups of edited plants.

In one group, the instructions for starting the protein were gone, along with the first 42 amino acids. Production in the other two stopped after 58 and 91 amino acids.

The edited plants still looked and flowered like the originals.

Two-day-old flowers then went into sealed jars, two flowers to a jar, and whatever they gave off over the next 24 hours was trapped and measured.

Without a working version of EOBV, the flowers released more eugenol, both forms of isoeugenol and vanillin. These compounds give cloves and vanilla their familiar aromas.

However, the flowers released less of almost every other scent compound, including methyl benzoate. The total amount of fragrance released also fell.

The team then ground up petals to measure how much of each compound remained inside. The clove and vanilla compounds had increased there, too.

The petals contained similar amounts of methyl benzoate and several other scent compounds even though the edited flowers released less of them.

Industry observers note that A repressor has to act on something, so the next question was which genes EOBV holds down. Gene activity was compared between edited and unedited flowers.

In a recent development, most indicated little difference. However, two genes, known as C4H2 and ADT3, became more active after the researchers removed EOBV.

C4H2 controls the carbon supply to the branch that produces eugenol, isoeugenol and vanillin.

The rise in C4H2 gene activity may help explain why the edited flowers made more eugenol, isoeugenol, and vanillin.

The team then tested that link directly. They connected the region of DNA that controls C4H2 activity to a system that produces red pigment.

In a recent development, petals that received EOBV showed no visible red color. Petals without the additional EOBV produced more than twice as much pigment.

Industry observers note that two other fragrance genes, PAAS and BSMT, became less active in the edited flowers. Since EOBV does not appear to bind directly to the regions controlling these genes, the changes were probably indirect.

Researchers found a similar pattern in 2011 when they reduced the activity of another petunia gene called PhMYB4. PhMYB4 and EOBV are about 80% identical. Genetic testing confirmed that PhMYB4 itself had not been edited.

According to recent reports, EOBV becomes more active when petunias grow in warmer conditions. The researchers wanted to see whether removing it could protect flowers from heat.

Recent findings suggest that they grew the plants in a greenhouse for a month before moving them into two rooms. The cooler room had temperatures of 72°F (22°C) during the day and 61°F (16°C) at night. The warmer room reached 82°F (28°C) and 72°F (22°C), respectively.

After measuring 38 flowers, the team found that unedited flowers became 12% narrower in warmer conditions. Edited flowers shrank by only 6%.

Recent findings suggest that heat also reduced the amount of scent released by unedited flowers, mainly due to lower emissions of benzaldehyde and methyl benzoate. Edited flowers maintained their overall scent output.

Meanwhile, PhEXP1, a gene that helps petal cells expand, became less active in both groups by similar amounts.

Heat-shrunk petunia flowers were traced to slower cell division in a 2021 study, a step this team did not measure.

More vanilla and clove compounds might sound appealing, but would these petunias actually smell better?

Nobody has asked people to smell the edited flowers. The researchers haven’t tested pollinators either.

Industry observers note that removing EOBV also has limits. In purple varieties, reducing EOBV activity left pigment levels unchanged.

EOBV belongs to the color machinery without fixing the shade of purple itself.

Sources indicate that the team also crossed the edited plants with petunias lacking EVER, another scent regulator. Those flowers did not outperform either parent. The authors suggest limited carbon, or a limited capacity to release scent.

The authors also disclosed a commercial interest. Skaliter and Vainstein are chief technology officer and chief scientific officer at CapsiBreed, which uses gene editing in hot and sweet peppers. Peppers and petunias are relatives.

One obvious next experiment is to switch EOBV off in plants that are already missing AN1 or AN11.

In a recent development, the team also wants to know whether other flowering plants are wired this way. And growers will want an answer to a blunter question: does a reshuffled scent give them flowers that anyone wants to buy?

The full study was published in the journal Plant Physiology.

#191709. Sitting behind the wheel may do something unusual to your heart rate

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1371 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Sitting behind the wheel may do something unusual to your heart rate

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1371 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Driving keeps the heart above its resting rate for longer, even when the body remains seated and inactive.
  • According to recent reports, sitting behind the wheel is usually treated as no different from sitting anywhere else.
  • During the time these people spent driving, their heart rates remained above resting level almost throughout.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Driving keeps the heart above its resting rate for longer, even when the body remains seated and inactive.

According to recent reports, sitting behind the wheel is usually treated as no different from sitting anywhere else. Heart-rate readings that were collected for a week from 57 young adults in Texas now suggest otherwise.

During the time these people spent driving, their heart rates remained above resting level almost throughout. A return to resting level was recorded about half as often as during other inactive hours.

Their hearts were not found to beat faster in the car than during those other hours. The resting pace was simply reached less often while a person was driving.

The study was designed and supervised by Ioannis Pavlidis who is a computer science professor at the University of Houston.

Colleagues from the same university and from the Texas A&M Transportation Institute worked with him.

Pavlidis said that a driver has to keep watching the road and deciding what to do next.

“The body may be sitting, but the mind is working,” he noted. According to him, it is in the heart rate that this mental work can be seen.

What the study isn’t able to show is that driving itself kept anyone’s heart rate up. The comparison that was made was between time spent driving and other inactive time in one week.

There are more differences between these two kinds of time than the car alone.

Posture and caffeine are on the list of them that the authors gave and so are passengers. How urgently a driver needed to arrive is on that list as well.

Recent findings suggest that the group consisted of 30 men and 27 women with an average age of about 26. Most of them were office workers.

A personal iPhone and Apple Watch were used by each participant from Monday through Sunday.

Every car was fitted with a small plug-in device by which each period of driving could be recorded. The watch was the source of the heart rate readings to which weather and traffic conditions were matched.

The rest of each day was labeled with the help of activity data from the phone and the watch. Any recorded minute in which a person was neither driving nor physically active was taken into the comparison.

Such minutes may have been spent at work or at home or somewhere else entirely.

The batteries of the iPhone and Apple Watch had usually run out by early evening. It is for this reason that the recordings cover daytime hours alone.

Sources indicate that it was Pavlidis’ group at the Affective and Data Computing Laboratory that averaged the readings minute by minute. The recordings that resulted came to 177,318 minutes which is close to 3,000 hours.

According to recent reports, no heart-rate reading existed for 13.6% of the driving minutes or for 3.5% of other inactive minutes. Neither speed nor traffic was found to be linked to the readings that were missing.

Driving took up about a tenth of that time. There were 973 trips in total and half of them were over within 15 minutes. A crash or a traffic ticket was generally not part of these drives.

Before any single minute could be judged, the team had to know each person’s resting heart rate.

An estimate of it is produced by the Apple Watch once a day. These daily estimates were averaged by the team across the whole week.

While a person was driving, their heart rate was above their own resting level 93.7% of the time on average. The figure for other inactive time was 81.3%.

Yet a higher heart rate in the car was not what the Houston team found. During driving, it averaged 11.2 beats per minute above resting level. The average for other inactive time was 11.5 beats above resting level.

A gap as small as that could have come up by chance.

Where driving did differ was in how little the heart rate varied. Its typical spread was 7.98 beats per minute during driving and 12.40 beats during other inactive time.

Heart rates dropped to resting level 2.46 times per hour during other inactive time and 1.31 times per hour while driving.

On weekdays, the two shares of time above resting level were 93.8% and 82.1%.

Weekends showed the same pattern, although people then spend their hours outside the car differently.

According to Pavlidis, a workout also raises heart rate, but the body becomes fitter as a result of it. From the time that is spent behind the wheel, no benefit of that kind is gained.

Yasmine Bouzid and the other authors also examined what a higher or lower heart rate was tied to.

During driving, there were two things that stood out from the rest. Time of day was the first since heart rates were higher in drives after noon than in the morning.

In a recent development, the second was the amount by which the driver’s wrist had turned in the minute before. The gyroscope of the Apple Watch supplied this measure which was treated as a sign of steering.

According to recent reports, away from the car, the list that was found was a broader one. On it were age and sex along with time of day and the Big Five personality trait of openness.

For this, the authors offered one reason which they regarded as possible. Driving is a single task whose demands remain fairly steady from one minute to the next.

Many different situations are covered by the inactive time that is spent away from the car.

Because a drive is repeated day after day, an example using anxiety was worked through by the team.

The volunteers had filled out the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, which scores a tendency to feel anxious from 20 to 80. The lowest score that was found in this group was 20 while the highest was 61.

It has been revealed that over every recorded minute of driving, the team’s heart-rate model was then run twice. A score of 20 was given to every driver in the first of these runs. In the second run, it was a score of 61 that every driver was given.

The heart rate that the model predicted with the score of 61 was higher by 0.99 beats per minute.

What the Houston team then did was to count such beats over a whole year. For a person who drives eight hours a day, the model projected about 173,000 extra heartbeats.

It came to roughly 11,000 extra heartbeats when the same was done for a 30-minute daily drive.

In a recent development, it was only as illustrations that these totals were described by Pavlidis and his coauthors. What they show is how a small difference accumulates, and not what anyone’s risk of heart disease is.

There were only young adults from Texas among the 57 volunteers, and none was followed for more than a week. Older drivers, professional drivers, or people with heart disease may not show the results that were found here.

It will take years of following drivers before the health side of this can be judged. Only then can it be learned whether more time above resting heart rate predicts heart problems.

Recent findings suggest that pavlidis noted that driving is something many people can’t do without. What his lab in Houston wants to find out is how the same trips could be made less demanding.

The Texas A&M Transportation Institute, where study co-author Michael Manser works, is supporting the lab through 2027.

The people who are to be studied next include long-distance commuters and those who drive for a living.

According to recent reports, rideshare drivers are an example of the latter. The groups are meant to be bigger, more varied, and followed for longer.

There is one more question that self-driving cars from Waymo and Tesla have raised for the lab. What does a rider’s heart rate do when it is the vehicle that handles the driving?

The full study was published in the journal npj Digital Public Health.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that sebnem Ece Eksi did a double take.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Industry observers note that sebnem Ece Eksi did a double take. Proteins typically studied in the brain were turning up in prostate cancer cells from high-risk patients. These proteins, called neuronal adhesion molecules, play a key role in the circuitry associated with memory.

Sources indicate that the finding, made during her Ph.D. days at the University of Illinois Chicago, raised so many questions to which Eksi is still seeking answers. Now at the Oregon Health & Science University in Portland, Eksi has made it her lab’s goal to find out how nervous systems communicate with cancer. What were once two separate fields might be connected more closely than previously thought.

“What we’re learning is that tumors are actively communicating with the nervous system,” Eksi notes. “In a way, it makes sense to me that a growing tumor in our bodies, in an organ, would be immediately sensed and detected by the nervous system.”.

Eksi now intends to test an AI image-based recognition algorithm to identify nerve fibers in human patients. This is exciting, she claims, because these nerves aren’t normally visible in patient tumors. But through biopsies, she hopes to map out and observe how the nervous system — which impacts sleep, cognition and pain — changes as cancer progresses. The implications are significant, she says. Could experts use the nervous system to detect cancer early? Can they improve patients’ quality of life?

“This field of cancer neuroscience can change all different stages of cancer diagnosis and treatments,” Eksi says. “It’s growing so quickly, the field itself.”.

Latest Update: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1055 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs waits to testify during her confirmation hearing with the Senate Commerce Committee on Tuesday.
  • President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.
  • Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs waits to testify during her confirmation hearing with the Senate Commerce Committee on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.

Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.

Much of the hearing focused on Carr and his threats to use the FCC to punish broadcasters he disagrees with.

Industry observers note that sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., noted that he expects Carr will not last long in his position once Democrats take control of Congress in the latest year.

“Mr. Carr, if you're listening now, know you're going to be in this body once a month, if not more, and in the House of Representatives as well, answering questions … so we can get to the bottom of the nonsense and the cover-ups that have been taking place,” Luján said.

Sources indicate that the nomination of Thumann Severs, who right now serves as senior counsel to Carr, has led to consternation among Democrats due to continued vacancies at the FCC. The five-member commission is intended to have three members of the president’s party, including the chair, and two in the minority.

It has been revealed that at the moment Carr serves alongside fellow Republican Olivia Trusty and Democrat Anna M. Gomez, whose term expired earlier this year. Gomez may continue to serve through next year under the law if a replacement is not nominated and confirmed.

Democrats are concerned that if Thumann Severs were to be confirmed, the commission’s three Republican members could constitute a quorum on their own, allowing Trump to fire Gomez.

In a recent development, sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., noted Senate precedent is to move pairs of one Democratic and one Republican nominee for the FCC and that he “strongly” believed the Thumann Severs nomination should have been paired with a renomination of Gomez in order to continue having “both parties at the table.”.

“A bipartisan FCC is essential to avoid things like large-scale media consolidation [and] I think also, more fundamentally, to protect a free and diverse press [that] serves everyone,” Hickenlooper said.

In addition to urging Trump to renominate Gomez, Democrats underlined the need for a second Democratic member of the commission.

Hickenlooper highlighted Thumann Severs’ close work with Carr, who Democrats and some Republicans have been critical of for comments about using the FCC’s public interest standard against television stations airing programming Carr disagrees with.

Thumann Severs’ work at the FCC presently focuses on the Wireline, Public Safety and Homeland Security, and Consumer and Governmental Affairs bureaus, rather than the Media Bureau.

Committee Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has also been critical of Carr’s comments. On Tuesday, he listed the FCC’s request for ABC-owned stations to submit early license renewals alongside earlier incidents in which he remarked Democrats encouraged the weaponization of the FCC against conservative voices.

“The First Amendment places vital limits on the government’s ability to regulate speech,” Cruz remarked. “The FCC possesses significant regulatory authority over communications, so there is always a risk that it could weaponize its authority against Americans with whom it disagrees.”.

Thumann Severs committed to Cruz that she would base licensing decisions on “the law and the record” and not use the FCC’s authority to “pressure or punish” broadcasters for protected speech.

According to recent reports, however, when Sen. Edward J. Markey, D-Mass., questioned Thumann Severs on whether the FCC could punish broadcasters the president disagreed with, Thumann Severs repeated one of Carr’s arguments in discussing the FCC’s role.

In a recent development, “Broadcasters are subject to public interest obligations as part of the public trustee model in exchange for the licenses that they hold,” she said. “As part of those public interest obligations, they are subject to many different rules and requirements, and the FCC is charged with enforcing and investigating the public interest standard against broadcasters.”.

Under repeated questions from Markey about Carr’s previous remarks, Thumann Severs stated she would base her decisions “in the facts and the law and the record.”.

In a recent development, luján also asked Thumann Severs to name issues where she had disagreed with Carr or Trump. While she stated her decisions would be her own, she declined to name any examples of disagreement.

In addition to questions about Carr, Democrats asked the nominee about the FCC’s E-Rate program, which provides low-cost connectivity for schools and libraries, and the Universal Service Fund, which funds the E-Rate program and other programs.

Thumann Severs stated that she believes the E-Rate program has been successful and that the FCC has a statutory obligation to provide some kind of discounted service to schools and libraries. But she was less forthcoming on whether the FCC could shut down the program as it currently exists without congressional approval or whether the program should be restricted only to rural areas.

Late last month, Democratic members of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, led by Communications and Technology Subcommittee ranking member Doris Matsui, D-Calif., sent a letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Cruz urging Gomez’s renomination with any move to confirm a Republican nominee.

In a recent development, “Commissioner Gomez has shown the experience and judgment to continue that work,” the members wrote. “We therefore ask that the Senate pair any newly introduced Republican nominee with her renomination to a full term, consistent with the bipartisan design Congress built into this agency.”.

On Monday, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights also sent a letter to committee leadership urging a delay on the hearing and any vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination until Gomez can be renominated.

“Independent agencies should not be extensions of presidential will: their leaders should exercise independent judgement based on their expertise and statutory mandates,” the group wrote.

Cruz did not indicate Tuesday when the committee might vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination, and no markup has yet been revealed by the committee of hers' and those of three others for two posts at NASA and one at the Transportation Department who also testified.

Latest Update: A con man claimed his secret gold mine was paying for a $2 million castle in Death Valley, but the mine never existed

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1317 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A man nicknamed "Death Valley Scotty" remarked his gold mine paid for Scotty's Castle.
  • In the 1920s, reporters who made the trip to a remote canyon in northern Death Valley found a Spanish-style mansion rising out of the desert.
  • According to recent reports, walter Scott, better known as “Death Valley Scotty,” had an explanation for it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A man nicknamed "Death Valley Scotty" remarked his gold mine paid for Scotty's Castle. That wasn't true. Here's what really happened.

In the 1920s, reporters who made the trip to a remote canyon in northern Death Valley found a Spanish-style mansion rising out of the desert.

According to recent reports, walter Scott, better known as “Death Valley Scotty,” had an explanation for it. He was building the two million dollar home, he mentioned, with profits from his secret gold mine.

According to recent reports, there was no mine. The house belonged to Albert Mussey Johnson, a Chicago insurance millionaire who had been sending Scotty money for years, according to the National Park Service.

When reporters asked Johnson about it, he agreed that Scotty owned the place and described himself simply as “Scotty’s banker.”.

A century later, the estate still carries the con man’s name. But Scotty’s Castle has been closed to regular visits since a flash flood in October 2015, and in October 2026 the park stated the earliest it could fully reopen is November 2028.

Scott was born in Kentucky in 1872. He ran away as a boy to join two of his brothers in Nevada, worked at the Harmony Borax Works and rode in Buffalo Bill Cody’s Wild West Show, according to the park.

After leaving the show in 1902, he turned to gold prospecting and convinced several wealthy businessmen that he had a claim to a fabulous gold mine in Death Valley.

Industry observers note that scott offered to split the profits if they first put up money to extract the ore. When no gold arrived, most of his investors decided they had been conned and backed out.

In July 1905, Scotty traveled by train to Chicago with a roll of money, falsely claiming to have struck it rich in a Death Valley mine. The trip broke the travel time record and opened doors among the wealthy elite.

According to the park’s biography of Johnson, he had already invested in Scotty’s mine in 1904, and he kept sending money even after the person he sent to check on Scott reported that there was no gold mine.

Recent findings suggest that in 1906, Johnson tried to visit the mine himself. On the way into the valley, his party was attacked in what became known as the Battle of Wingate Pass, and Scotty’s brother Warner was shot. The park describes Scotty as a flamboyant con artist and showman.

When Johnson finally made it to Death Valley, Scotty took him on a grueling trek by horseback, apparently expecting the desert to be too much for him.

Johnson had been badly injured in a train accident in his youth. Instead, he stayed nearly a month, and his health improved dramatically in the dry, sunny climate.

Sources indicate that he never saw the mine and was almost certainly being swindled, the park states, but he did not seem to mind. The two men became lifelong friends.

Johnson went on to buy land in spring-fed Grapevine Canyon, about 3,000 feet above sea level, eventually owning 1,500 acres.

His wife, Bessie, suggested building something more comfortable than the canvas tents they had been using, so they could “get away from the rattlesnakes and scorpions.”.

Work on what they called Death Valley Ranch began in the 1920s, and the garage built in 1922 served as the workshop for the construction.

Industry observers note that scotty, who recognized a good story, told everyone the house was his. Even the concrete posts along the property’s fence were stamped with an “S” for Scotty and a “J” for Johnson, the true owner.

Construction stopped in 1931, when Johnson discovered that, because of a surveying error, he had been building on federal land.

Sources indicate that the Great Depression was beginning to take hold, and the work never resumed. The castle was left incomplete, and its swimming pool was never finished.

Johnson died in 1948 and left most of his fortune and property to the Gospel Foundation, which he had founded two years earlier.

Sources indicate that scotty had the right to live at the castle for the rest of his life. He died in January 1954. Johnson had hoped the National Park Service would one day buy the property, and in 1970 it did.

For decades, rangers in period costume led tours through the house and told the story of the Johnsons and their friend.

On the night of October 18, 2015, Scotty’s Castle received 2 3/4 inches of rain, about a year’s worth, in five hours, after a half-inch the day before.

In a recent development, A flash flood of mud and rocks poured down Grapevine Canyon at an estimated 3,200 cubic feet per second, according to the park. On steep slopes like these, heavy rain can trigger flash floods faster than expected.

Rangers sheltered with about 20 stranded visitors on the rim of Ubehebe Crater that night, and one ranger watched power poles and metal dumpsters float out of the canyon. Nobody was hurt.

The main house mostly escaped the flood. The historic garage, which served as the visitor center, did not. The water broke through its windows, doors and walls and left four feet of mud and rocks inside.

The unfinished pool filled many feet deep with mud and debris, and most of the 8-mile road through the canyon was destroyed.

In a recent development, repairs were under way in April 2021 when contractors arrived one morning to find the garage on fire, with flames spreading to the neighboring Longshed. The garage was destroyed.

A state investigation found the fire started inside the building but could not determine a cause and found no evidence of arson.

Sources indicate that the park has given two figures for how far the garage repairs had gone, 37% in a June 2021 release and 60% on its recovery page. One of the upgrades being installed was fire sprinklers.

In 2019, the park expected to reopen the castle in October 2021. After the fire, the target moved to 2023. It is now November 2028 at the earliest.

The park lists funding and staffing problems, legal reviews to protect historic and natural features, contracting complications, unforeseen conditions, the pandemic, more flooding and the fire.

The repairs cost about $71 million, split into separate projects so they could be funded from different sources.

Some of the work is done. New berms and flood walls finished in January 2023 protected the historic district when the remnants of Hurricane Hilary hit the park that August. The road through the canyon has been rebuilt.

The next phase, expected to start in 2027, covers the parking lot, the Longshed and the historic Gas Tank House, which will become a small visitor contact station in place of the burned garage.

After that, curators will return the furnishings and museum collections to the house before interior tours can resume.

Industry observers note that until then, the only way in is a guided tour. This season, rangers and guides from the Death Valley Natural History Association are leading exterior tours of the grounds on most Saturdays and Sundays through April 17.

Industry observers note that tickets are sold through the association. Bonnie Clare Road, the 8-mile route through Grapevine Canyon, remains closed to the public, including pedestrians.

Once the castle is fully reopened, the park looks to open it each year from late fall through early spring.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s October 2026 announcement on Scotty’s Castle tours, its pages on the Scotty’s Castle flood and recovery, building the castle, Death Valley Scotty, Albert Mussey Johnson and the showmen of Death Valley tourism, and its releases on the 2021 fire, the fire investigation and the repairs four years after the flood.

The 6 Best Mini-LED TVs Deliver a Bright Screen and Great Value

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Industry observers note that mini-LED is among the most versatile display technologies ever created.
  • The best mini-LED TVs right now provide a brighter and more impactful picture than ever, especially since many of them get a performance boost from other display tech like quantum dots and the hot latest multicolored backlight configuration, RGB LED.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that mini-LED is among the most versatile display technologies ever created. By shrinking down the LED backlighting that powered older TVs since flat screens first gained traction in the late 2000s, TV makers have found a way to deliver brighter TVs with richer, more accurate colors without relying on expensive newly introduced display technologies.

The best mini-LED TVs right now provide a brighter and more impactful picture than ever, especially since many of them get a performance boost from other display tech like quantum dots and the hot latest multicolored backlight configuration, RGB LED.

According to recent reports, just as importantly, they often offer great bang for the buck, especially when you're looking for a larger screen size—let’s say 75 inches or higher. As malleable as they are cost-effective, mini-LED is the secret sauce behind some of the best TVs on the market, even outdoing premium OLED screens in metrics like brightness and color expansion.

We’ve tested the top mini-LED TVs around, from entry-level options to groundbreaking flagships, to help you find the best options for your money.

I picked the top mini-LED TVs after sampling the best the market has to offer from brands like LG, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Hisense. I tested four of the TVs directly, while two of them were tested by Popular Mechanics staff and recommended based on that testing.

Sources indicate that my evaluation was based on performance traits like brightness, color vibrancy and accuracy, image processing and upscaling, black levels, and overall contrast. For my testing process, I used objective measurements like brightness and color accuracy with a Portrait Displays C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, a G1 pattern generator, and Calman software, as well as subjective testing using a wide library of familiar content, from test demos to films and TV highlights via 4K HDR Blu-rays and streaming. I also weighed usability features like smarts and gaming options, overall design, and size options for those interested in the ever-expanding massive-screen TV market.

According to recent reports, I’ve been reviewing TVs and audio technology for well over a decade at publications like Wired, Business Insider, Digital Trends, and others. I’ve reviewed virtually every kind of TV and display technology available, from budget screens to premium RGB LEDs. I’ve gone hands-on with the best new mini-LED TVs from brands like Samsung, LG, Sony, TCL, Hisense, Roku, and others, along with competing tech like OLED and QD-OLED, each of which has its advantages. Few things give me more pleasure than finding people the best tech for their money at every performance level and budget.

RGB LED, which uses tri-colored red, green, and blue light clusters for enhanced color expression, was the hot upcoming display tech at the start of 2026. Virtually every major brand debuted some form of RGB Mini-LED, kick-starting a premium Mini-LED alternative to OLED.

Sources indicate that when TCL introduced its own RGB TV for 2026, the RM9L, it seemed less excited about the RGB factor, and more interested in hyping up its exclusive upcoming mini-LED tech, Super Quantum Dots (SQD). The QM8L makes it easy to see why.

According to recent reports, SQD is an advanced version of regular quantum dots: tiny nanocrystals that emit pure, bright colors when exposed to light to enhance colors and brightness. Fancy tech aside, the results speak for themselves. The QM8L offers incredible brightness, far outshining its predecessor, the QM8K, alongside expansive colors that are as accurate as they are vibrant.

It has been revealed that the newly introduced display offers other benefits, including fantastic black levels with very little light bleed, and reduced off-angle performance loss for most settings. Image processing has also improved, getting closer to the clarity and upscaling in top flagships from brands like LG and Samsung. The result is a premium picture that comes tantalizingly close to OLED displays in terms of contrast between the lightest and darkest images, and details that seem to pull you into the screen.

The TV’s Google TV interface is another plus, offering easy setup and extras like the ability to add albums from your Google Photos library as screen savers. Modern connectivity provides top-tier gaming features across inputs, and the sound isn’t bad either, thanks to built-in Bang & Olufsen speakers. Given that you can grab a 65-inch QM8L for as low as $1,000 or less on sale, it’s an easy pick for the best mini-LED TV available.

In many ways, entry-level TVs like the Hisense U6SF Pro are the best way to gauge how far TV tech has come in recent years. You just don’t expect a TV this cheap to look this good, from punchy brightness and naturalistic colors to minimal light bleed that lets you watch even challenging scenes in a dark room without being pulled out of the moment.

One sacrifice at this price is the TV’s black levels, which don’t look as rich as pricier mini-LED TVs, let alone self-lit OLED displays. Because of that, even though the TV’s brightness rises above anything you can stream, it can look less striking than step-up models. On the other hand, its matte-like screen does a great job of diminishing ambient light and even direct light reflections for a good picture day or night. That’s something I didn’t expect to see at this level.

You’ll get some handy features, including support for all major HDR formats and dual HDMI 2.1 ports with VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) up to 144 Hz for PC gaming, another impressive get at this price. I find the TV’s Fire TV smart system a little clunky, but it includes some cool extras, like Ambient Mode that displays free artwork. TCL’s QM6K is a good alternative thanks to its friendlier Google TV smart system, but it can’t match the U6SF Pro’s performance, which is the best I’ve tested at its price point.

Industry observers note that the step-down model of our top-rated QM8L, TCL’s QM7L offers many of the same goodies that make its pricier sibling such a rock star, but at a much lower list price. It all starts with the same SQD display tech, for excellent brightness and color vibrancy, and the kind of dimensional contrast that pushes mini-LED closer to OLED.

The QM7L isn’t quite as much of a powerhouse as the QM8L, but it’s still put-on-your-sunglasses bright, blasting well past anything you can stream, and properly lighting high-quality 4K HDR Blu-rays. Its potency aids in remarkable color expansion for a deep dive into advanced films like Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse. Importantly, the TV also provides good color accuracy, along with deep black levels for excellent contrast. You’ll still see some minor light bleed if you look for it, and picture quality is reduced off-axis, but both are relatively minor concessions, especially for the price.

It has been revealed that the TV offers a similarly loaded set of gaming features to last year’s QM7K, including options like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) and ALLM (Auto Low Latency Mode) across two of its four HDMI inputs. Like the QM8L, its Google TV smart system is intuitive to set up and use. That’s all icing on a TV that comes about as close as I’ve seen to a premium display for the money.

Hisense’s mid-tier mini-LED TV doesn’t offer the latest display technologies like RGB LED or Super Quantum Dots, but it does offer seriously punchy performance, along with a design that feels much more premium than its price class suggests. That starts with Hisense’s latest anti-reflective matte screen that eliminates most ambient reflections, matched by slim bezels and a stylish pedestal stand with the kind of build quality usually reserved for flagship TVs.

In a recent development, under the hood is a potent mini-LED display that employs regular quantum dots for rich colors and brightness that meets or beats anything in its class, including TCL’s QM7L. When paired with its rich black levels and reflection-repelling screen, you’ll have no trouble watching even darker shows in a bright room. Hisense’s image processing has also improved for enhanced detail and upscaling with low-quality content. I did notice that the TV’s local dimming may create some artifacts at its highest setting, but it’s a very minor issue. Like most backlit TVs, it also loses some picture quality when viewed from an angle.

Feature-wise, the U7SG is a gaming master, including VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 165 Hz across all four HDMI inputs, and handy extras like an intuitive game bar for adjusting settings on the fly. Add in its snappy Google TV interface, and you’re getting a whole lot of good stuff at a price that often falls well below $1,000 for a 65-inch model, and stays competitive up to a whopping 116 inches.

Industry observers note that after skipping a year, Hisense’s flagship U9 series is back, now loaded with the latest RGB LED display tech for a striking makeover. The TV uses its tri-colored red, green, and blue mini-LED backlighting to great effect, providing rich black levels and sparkling colors that increasingly close the gap with OLED, alongside the kind of dazzling brightness that OLED can’t yet match.

Recent findings suggest that the UR9’s screen gets an advanced version of Hisense’s matte-like anti-glare coating called “Obsidian,” which impressively repels ambient and even most direct light sources, making it a great option in sunlit rooms. Turn the lights off, and you’ll find great shadow detail and very little light bleed from bright objects on dark backgrounds.

Industry observers note that hisense outfits the TV with some premium extras, from a capable 4.1.2-channel speaker system to HDMI 2.1 support at up to 165 Hz across all three HDMI inputs. There’s also a DisplayPort for connecting a PC, though I would have liked to see a fourth HDMI 2.1 port as well. The TV has also gotten an enhancement for the latest advanced HDR format, Dolby Vision 2, making it well-primed for the future. It’s all wrapped in a stylish design, for a posh taste of next-gen luxury at an accessible price point.

In a recent development, TCL was so confident in its entry-level QM6K that it was the first TV the brand released with its newly introduced mini-LED display tech in 2025, and the only major model that wasn’t replaced for 2026. That badge of honor is well earned, as the QM6K is one of the best-performing TVs I’ve tested in its price class, with naturalistic colors, rich black levels and contrast, and enough brightness to properly light up HDR scenes like a blazing sunset or a jet’s afterburners.

Recent findings suggest that maybe just as impressive are the challenges the QM6K avoids. While most TVs in its class readily reveal issues like screen aberrations on solid backgrounds, light bleed from bright images, and awful off-angle performance, the QM6K mostly stays clear of those pitfalls so you can simply enjoy the picture without distraction. My only real performance complaint is the TV’s particularly bad sound, but given that nearly all TVs I test are much better off with a soundbar or speaker system, that’s not a big surprise.

It has been revealed that when it comes to extras, the QM6K is well stocked with options like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 144 Hz for blur-free action and a gaming bar to adjust features on the fly. And while the TV isn’t nearly as bright as my top budget pick, the U6SF Pro, its Google TV smart system is more intuitive and responsive for a better overall user experience. With a 55-inch model now available for under $500, the QM6K is tough to pass up.

Most TVs on this list are available from 55 inches to large-scale models at 98 inches or larger, and at increasingly reasonable price points. A major reason for that is, unlike OLED, mini-LED TVs are scalable at a relatively low cost, so screens fit for large home theaters are much more attainable. That’s one of mini-LED’s biggest advantages over other display tech, not to mention the potential for next-gen brightness and color coverage at lower pricing. That said, ultra-large screens more readily expose performance issues, so it’s notable to balance screen size with quality so you don’t regret your purchase later.

It has been revealed that all of the TVs on this list offer 4K resolution with HDR (High Dynamic Range), and you wouldn’t want to buy a TV with lower resolution these days unless you’re looking for a very small screen (around 48 inches or lower) for a bedroom or office. The majority of new content is shot in 4K with HDR, the latter of which provides higher brightness and better contrast between the lightest and darkest images, along with the potential for more vibrant colors. Some TVs still offer 8K resolution, but because 8K content is scarce and difficult to recognize with the naked eye, it’s essentially dead (or at least dormant) in the current TV landscape.

Recent findings suggest that as for refresh rates, any TV with 120-Hz or higher is preferred for fast-moving content like sports and, especially, gaming. All of the TVs on this list offer 120 Hz refresh rates or higher with VRR (Variable Refresh Rate), designed to adjust to games dynamically to reduce lag and screen tearing/blur. Many TVs push to 144 Hz or better, but those refresh rates are only accessible with select gaming PCs. For consoles—PS5, Xbox Series S/X, and the Nintendo Switch 2—120 Hz is sufficient.

Industry observers note that all of the displays on this list use mini-LED-backlighting, a smaller and more accurate version of traditional LED backlighting, paired with a liquid-crystal display (LCD). Because mini-LEDs are smaller, they can be used more prevalently to create better brightness and more dimming zones, which can enhance black levels for better contrast between the brightest and darkest images. Mini-LEDs can also be enhanced by features like quantum dots, nanoparticles that produce pure bright colors when exposed to light. Some advanced Mini-LED TVs also use RGB LED technology, which trades uniform blue or white mini-LEDs for multicolor red, green, and blue light clusters designed to produce purer, more expansive colors at the light source.

In a recent development, in contrast (no pun intended), OLED displays use organic material excited by electricity to light each of a TV’s millions of pixels independently. These self-lit (a.k.a. self-emissive) displays have distinct advantages, including the ability to create perfect black levels for enhanced contrast over backlit displays, along with much wider viewing angles. Like mini-LEDs, some OLED displays also use quantum dots: So-called “QD-OLED” TVs offer enhanced brightness and colors, among other new technologies to compete with ever-brighter and more advanced mini-LED TVs.

Recent findings suggest that both display types have their advantages. OLED is the best choice for those after a more balanced, nuanced, and uniform picture, especially if money isn’t a concern. However, because mini-LED is generally cheaper to produce, it may be a better choice for those on a budget who want the largest and brightest screen for their money. And in recent years, the best mini-LED TVs have increasingly advanced to better compete against OLED.

In a recent development, the most notable connectivity option for gamers is HDMI 2.1, which offers higher bandwidth to get the most out of gaming devices. HDMI 2.1 allows for high refresh rates and features like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) from devices like the PS5, Xbox Series X, and gaming PCs. If you’re only connecting a Blu-ray player or streaming device, HDMI 2.0 will suffice. All of the TVs on this list also support HDMI eARC/ARC, which allows you to easily connect newer soundbars and other audio devices at high resolution for enhanced audio performance.

WiFi 6 or 7 may also be helpful for wireless streaming, especially if you’re watching a lot of high-resolution content, though you’ll need a router that supports those formats. Most TVs also include an Ethernet connection for a mainline connection to your modem. Other connection options to consider include Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, ATSC 3.0 for features like over-the-air HDR from an HD antenna, and an optical connection for older audio devices like a legacy amplifier or soundbar.

Recent findings suggest that all the TVs on this list come with a smart TV platform for streaming from popular apps, and many include options that let you stream content directly from a smartphone like Apple AirPlay or Google Cast. My favorite platforms are Roku and Google TV, which I find the easiest to navigate and use on a daily basis. All smart platforms collect some form of personal information, so it’s crucial to be careful when agreeing to terms and licensing to protect your privacy.

Industry observers note that each TV also supports multiple HDR formats, which is crucial for getting the best performance. HDR10 is the baseline format, which all modern TVs support. Most TVs also support dynamic HDR formats like Dolby Vision and HDR10+ (many support both). These advanced formats can provide a more precise vision of a director’s intent by adjusting the brightest and darkest images scene by scene, and even frame by frame. Dolby Vision is the most common dynamic HDR format for streaming.

Industry observers note that if you’re interested in voice control, you’ll want to look for voice assistants like Roku Voice, Amazon Alexa or Alexa+, and Google Assistant or Gemini. If you’re connecting an audio device that supports spatial audio, like a Dolby Atmos soundbar or A/V receiver, you may also want to ensure your TV supports 3D audio formats like Dolby Atmos and, for 4K Blu-rays, DTS:X.

The second most common element in the universe is actually running out here on Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, most of the elements we rely on were found underground, but helium was first discovered in space.
  • Recent findings suggest that most of the elements we rely on were found underground, but helium was first discovered in space.
  • The British scientist Norman Lockyer named the mystery substance helium after Helios, the Greek god of the Sun, as recounted by the American Physical Society.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, most of the elements we rely on were found underground, but helium was first discovered in space. In 1868, astronomers studying a total solar eclipse spotted a mysterious….

Recent findings suggest that most of the elements we rely on were found underground, but helium was first discovered in space. In 1868, astronomers studying a total solar eclipse spotted a mysterious yellow band in the Sun’s light spectrum that did not match any known element.

The British scientist Norman Lockyer named the mystery substance helium after Helios, the Greek god of the Sun, as recounted by the American Physical Society.

Humanity had identified an element in starlight 93 million miles (150 million kilometers) away before anyone held a sample of it.

Confirmation took decades. The Scottish chemist William Ramsay finally isolated terrestrial helium in 1895, releasing it from a uranium-bearing mineral nearly 27 years after Lockyer first saw its signature.

Sources indicate that that long delay hints at the problem now reshaping hospitals and laboratories. Helium is the second-most-abundant element in the universe, yet it is genuinely rare on Earth.

Industry observers note that the contradiction comes down to gravity. Helium is so light that it drifts upward, escapes the atmosphere, and is lost to space forever. Our Moon even collects traces of the gases our planet sheds. The cosmic abundance simply never settled here.

The helium we use does not come from the Big Bang reservoir that fills the cosmos. It forms underground, atom by atom, as radioactive uranium and thorium decay within the crust.

Those elements decay on almost unimaginable timescales. Uranium-238 has a half-life of about 4.5 billion years and thorium-232 closer to 14 billion years, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Each decay releases the alpha particles that become helium.

The same slow chemistry that shaped Earth’s crust over billions of years also governs its helium. No factory can shortcut that process, which is why no large-scale method exists to manufacture the gas artificially.

In a recent development, this is the deeper reason the current squeeze matters. A shortfall in most materials invites more mining or more production. A helium shortfall invites neither, because the planet replenishes its supply only as fast as atoms decay.

Producers extract helium as a trace component of natural gas, and only deposits with high enough concentrations are worth tapping. That narrow geology leaves the market exposed to plant shutdowns and trade disruptions.

The strain is already visible. Hospitals consume roughly a third of the world’s helium to cool the superconducting magnets in MRI scanners, and analysts expect global demand to double by 2035 as semiconductor and electric-vehicle manufacturing expand.

Sources indicate that the hunt for fresh supply is reaching parts of the world that never produced helium before. In Tanzania, the Southern Rukwa project finalized its mining agreements in May 2026, positioning the country to extract helium at a commercial scale. Qatar has also moved to bring newly introduced capacity online.

Policy decisions have added uncertainty. The United States sold its Federal Helium System, once the planet’s largest single source, to the industrial gas tech giant Messer in June 2024, ending nearly a century of public stewardship, the U.S. Bureau of Land Management confirmed.

According to recent reports, newer MRI machines now seal and recirculate their helium, and many labs capture and re-liquefy every drop they can. These measures buy time, much as a simple scan can buy a patient time. Whether they arrive fast enough is the open question.

Industry observers note that there is a quiet symmetry to the helium story. We discovered it by looking up at a star, much as a meteorite can reveal a vanished world, and we may yet preserve it by looking down into the rocks that hoard it.

Sources indicate that for now, the element that fills birthday balloons remains one of the most strategically important substances on the planet. It reminds us that some of Earth’s rarest things are those we first noticed in the heavens.

The full study was published in the journal Physics Today.

#191702. Crews tearing up a 1950s parking lot at Dinosaur National Monument hit fossils, but the real find was a dinosaur tail with nine vertebrae

Crews tearing up a 1950s parking lot at Dinosaur National Monument hit fossils, but the real find was a dinosaur tail with nine vertebrae

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1111 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Under a Dinosaur National Monument parking lot, a paleontologist found a likely Diplodocus tail with nine vertebrae in the first dig there since 1924.
  • Industry observers note that in September 2025, road crews at Dinosaur National Monument in Utah peeled back the asphalt outside the Quarry Exhibit Hall, the most popular stop in the park.
  • Over the next five weeks, the job turned into a dinosaur dig.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Under a Dinosaur National Monument parking lot, a paleontologist found a likely Diplodocus tail with nine vertebrae in the first dig there since 1924.

Industry observers note that in September 2025, road crews at Dinosaur National Monument in Utah peeled back the asphalt outside the Quarry Exhibit Hall, the most popular stop in the park. They were there to rebuild a parking lot. The first scoop of the backhoe brought up pieces of fossil bone.

Over the next five weeks, the job turned into a dinosaur dig.

Park paleontologist ReBecca Hunt-Foster and her assistant followed a trail of bones through the rock until they had uncovered nine tail vertebrae and the leg and arm bones of a long-necked dinosaur, most likely Diplodocus.

Its relatives still turn up in surprising places, including the first Diplodocus ever found outside North America.

It has been revealed that it was the first fossil excavation in that part of the historic Carnegie Quarry since 1924, the National Park Service stated. In an account published this fall, Hunt-Foster described how the last bones of the tail were lying right against the old asphalt.

In a recent development, the spot has a long history. On August 17, 1909, Earl Douglass, a paleontologist from the Carnegie Museum in Pittsburgh, spotted eight dinosaur tailbones sticking out of a sandstone ledge in the Utah desert. “It was a beautiful sight,” he wrote in his diary.

His crews spent the next 13 years digging there and collected more than 317 metric tons of fossils and rock between 1909 and 1922, according to Hunt-Foster, much of it shipped back to Pittsburgh.

The Smithsonian dug on the east side of the quarry in 1923, and the University of Utah in 1924. In 1915, President Woodrow Wilson set aside the quarry and 80 acres around it as Dinosaur National Monument.

According to recent reports, all that digging produced a lot of waste rock. It was dumped off the eastern side of the quarry, and in the 1930s, Fresh Deal work crews cleared more debris while improving the road.

Those tailing piles later became the parking lot for the Quarry Exhibit Hall, which opened in 1958 around a wall of rock where visitors can see about 1,500 dinosaur fossils still in place.

In May 2025, the park was due to begin an $11.2 million project to upgrade roads, parking areas and overlooks along the route to the Quarry Exhibit Hall.

Because the work crossed fossil-bearing rock, the park brought on a seasonal paleontological assistant, Rudolph Hummel, to watch the construction.

The biggest worry was the parking lot. Fossils overlooked by the early excavators, or judged not worth keeping, could be sitting in the old tailings. The bone-bearing sandstone itself might also turn up.

The road and the exhibit hall closed from September 8 to late October 2025. Monitoring in the parking lot began on September 10, after the asphalt cap came off.

On September 11, the team found the first identifiable bone, a vertebra from a meat-eating dinosaur, likely Allosaurus. Smaller finds followed every day as the crew dug down five feet. Construction sites have a way of turning up fossils, as a Los Angeles project indicated.

The construction workers got caught up in it too. Many of them jumped in to search for fossils by hand rather than by backhoe alone, Hunt-Foster wrote, and one worker spent two days power-washing a section of the sandstone so it could be studied.

On September 16, after that washing was done, Hunt-Foster was documenting the exposed sandstone when she spotted a fossil bone in its cross section.

It turned out to be a large limb bone plunging down into the rock. Construction in that corner of the lot was paused.

Industry observers note that after a week of digging, the pair found a tail vertebra lying over the long bone, which they identified as a sauropod tibia. Then a second vertebra appeared, and a third, all still connected. Hummel followed them east while Hunt-Foster worked west.

Six more tail vertebrae turned up, along with the bones of the lower arm. By then, the team had concluded that the tail likely belonged to Diplodocus, the most abundant dinosaur in the Carnegie Quarry.

They also found a partial turtle, plenty of freshwater clams and carbonized wood lying directly under the skeleton.

According to recent reports, by September 26, the team had reached the end of the tail. The vertebrae grew smaller toward the east, and the last one was missing its back half, cleanly sheared off and tilted up toward the old surface.

It has been revealed that hunt-Foster and Hummel suspect that the tip of the tail, if it was preserved at all, was plowed off when the road was first built in the late 1950s. Several of the last vertebrae were in direct contact with the asphalt from the lot’s first paving.

Photos from the visitor center’s opening on June 1, 1958, show the lot was still gravel, and it does not appear to have been paved until around 1959, she wrote.

All of this happened while the fresh parking lot was being built around the dig. Dump trucks full of fill rolled past and rollers packed down the ground around them. “In a short amount of time, we were sitting in a deep trench surrounded by a fresh parking lot,” Hunt-Foster wrote.

Volunteers, a Utah Conservation Corps crew, park coworkers and construction staff helped wrap the bones in protective field jackets. The first small jacket came out on October 13. On October 17, the construction crew’s backhoe operator lifted out the rest.

It has been revealed that in all, about 3,000 pounds of fossils and rock came out of the 2025 dig. The bones are now being cleaned and studied at the Utah Field House of Natural History State Park Museum in Vernal, Utah.

Visitors can watch the work in the museum’s fossil preparation lab. Some fossils from the excavation are also on display at the Quarry Exhibit Hall.

The parking lot is finished, and the Quarry Exhibit Hall is open daily except on Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s Day.

The story is not over. Hunt-Foster states a second part of her account will cover continued excavation work in 2026 and additional discoveries.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s January 2026 announcement of the excavation, ReBecca Hunt-Foster’s article The Parking Lot Sauropod of Dinosaur National Monument: Part 1 in Park Paleontology News, and the park’s pages on Earl Douglass and the historic Carnegie Quarry.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • Sources indicate that think about the phrase “it’s just like riding a bicycle.” At first, it’s hard, and you have to pay attention to what you’re doing, but after you’ve practiced for many hours, bike riding becomes so natural you don’t even have to think about it; you just hop on and go.
  • According to recent reports, intuition is about finding the solution automatically and without deep thought, notes Wim De Neys, a cognitive psychologist and CNRS research professor at the University of Paris.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

Sources indicate that think about the phrase “it’s just like riding a bicycle.” At first, it’s hard, and you have to pay attention to what you’re doing, but after you’ve practiced for many hours, bike riding becomes so natural you don’t even have to think about it; you just hop on and go. In fact, you can hardly explain how you learned in the first place or exactly how you’re keeping your balance as you pedal on. You just trust your body to do it. The same applies to cognitive activities: As a child, you had to really think about how to arrive at the answer of 2+2, but now, you just know it’s four, without thinking.

According to recent reports, intuition is about finding the solution automatically and without deep thought, notes Wim De Neys, a cognitive psychologist and CNRS research professor at the University of Paris. At its core, your intuition is a behavior your brain develops based on patterns and experiences over time, a kind of automation for something you’ve done countless times. That’s why intuition is often linked to expertise. Trusting your gut may sound ill-advised, so why wouldn’t you want to think things through? But it turns out that generating your instincts for decision-making can both help you make the right choice in times of confusion and stress, and also free up mental resources for other tasks.

So, can you train your intuition to sense better choices?

According to recent reports, well, it’s not that simple, according to De Neys, whose research focuses on how intuitive and deliberate thinking develops over our lifetimes. You can’t sidestep the deep reflection needed to build the foundation of your intuitions. But you can tap into them in a more meaningful way, especially over time.

“Having gut feelings and intuition and even valid intuitions, there’s science to back it up,” De Neys notes. “It exists, but it’s always tied to expertise, and expertise means it’s something that you’ve done a lot.”.

Industry observers note that intuition isn’t some overall sense; instead it’s tied to one area of expertise, like an interviewer being able to pick up on the candidate who’ll be the right fit for the job, or an experienced doctor delivering a diagnosis. While you won’t have expert intuition about everything under the sun, there are a few ways you can boost your own decision-making.

First, you need to get better at pattern matching, and that means practice. Intuition is tied to pattern-matching, Jeff Larsen, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains. For example, chess masters earn their distinction by practicing so much that when they see the board, they don’t have to stop and think about what the two or three best moves will be. Others with less expertise may watch a game and think, “that was a silly move,” but they don’t realize the master player has spent years building up pattern recognition, or an accurate gut feeling, Larsen explains.

Sources indicate that second, stop second-guessing your intuition. You can do this by asking yourself, “How might I be wrong?” One approach is to ask a friend who may disagree with you or might have an outside perspective. This can also help you understand that, often, an instinctual choice you made in the heat of the moment is correct. Even if the choice isn’t exactly right, it’s probably good enough to keep you safe. For example, when you’re driving down the interstate, you have some intuition about whether you can make a lane change or not, and whether you need to slow down or speed up to avoid an accident. Thinking about the consequences of your decision-making can also help give you more confidence in your intuition.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes you have to trust your gut on a truly life-changing decision. When it comes to marriage, the information overload can sometimes feel overwhelming. However, when it comes to close relationships, you’ve presumably experienced many behavioral exchanges with your partner, and this allows for substantial information-gathering to “feed your gut,” Michael Olson, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains.

It has been revealed that since you can’t possibly keep this massive load of information in your conscious memory at all times, it translates into a neat summary of all those behavioral exchanges. Now you have a gut feeling that this person is right for you—or not.

Industry observers note that and the research agrees. A study Olson coauthored, published in Science, found that the “explicit,” or “conscious” evaluations couples in the study made of their partners while in the so-called initial “honeymoon stage” didn’t mean as much when stretched over four years. Instead, those who reported positive gut feelings over this time period had a more accurate idea of their happiness in their relationship.

According to recent reports, your gut doesn’t just extend to your love life. Trusting it can also help you to be successful in business. Elizabeth Rea, an evidentiary clairvoyant psychic medium, now teaches established founders and CEOs to tap into their own intuitions, through her company, Insightful. As a medium, Rea has also assisted U.S. federal special agents investigating cold murder cases.

When working with clients, she asks them to relax what they consciously believe. Sometimes so-called gut feelings may come to us in the form of chills down our spine or another physical sensation. But since we’re living in a left-brained culture that prizes making decisions using logic and analysis, those instincts often get passed off as coincidences and ignored, Rea claims. Sometimes, gut feelings may also be ignored because of self-doubt. Your intuition often whispers to you, she tells clients. Honing these signals will help you improve your self-trust—thereby improving your intuition.

In a recent development, overall, training yourself to trust your intuition will help you become a better decision-maker. You’ll make the right choices without the agonizing process of picking through pros and cons and running scenarios in your brain for days on end.

It has been revealed that “It’s a lot more cost-efficient if we can offload [decision-making] to our intuition,” De Neys states. “Often that’s going to be helpful because then it frees up resources for something else that might be more important at that point in time.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper.
  • Glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 22: Flat-floored lunar crater Schickard.

According to recent reports, A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper. Cepheus is home to several lovely double stars, including Xi (ξ) Cephei, also known as Kurhah.

Glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base. You can find it about midway between Alderamin (Alpha [α] Cep) and Iota (ι) Cep, the western and eastern points in the house’s box, respectively. Kurhah’s two components are separated by just under 8” — once you find the star in binoculars or your finder scope, any telescope will split them. The pair consists of a brighter magnitude 4.4 primary, which glows white, and a fainter magnitude 6.5 secondary, which appears to many observers as yellow.

Sources indicate that if you happen to have a large telescope, you may want to give a nearby deep-sky treasure a try: planetary nebula NGC 7139 sits just 2° west-southwest of Kurhah, but it requires a large scope (8 inches at least) to spot, as this bubble of gas glows at magnitude 13.3. If available, an Oxygen-III filter will help bring it out by dimming the nearby stars.

Industry observers note that sunrise: 6:54 A.M.Sunset: 4:38 P.M.Moonrise: 3:37 P.M.Moonset: 5:52 A.M.Moon Phase: Full*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST on November 24, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. A Super Moon occurs when the Moon reaches Full phase close to perigee, its closest point to Earth, making our satellite appear larger and brighter than average. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon. A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars.

This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope (just note that you may want a Moon filter if available, as our satellite is so substantial and bright). The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

The 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed rapidly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. The latter two may be difficult to catch from the Midwest without optical aid, as sunrise is fast approaching. If you are using binoculars or a telescope in this region, make sure to put them away several minutes ahead of sunrise from your location. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

It has been revealed that alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.
